content: Healthcare facilities should establish and implement clear triage policies to enable rapid screening and assessment of potential MERS-CoV cases, as well as all cases presenting with acute respiratory symptoms. It is essential for healthcare workers to consistently apply standard precautions with all patients, regardless of their diagnosis, in all work practices at all times. When caring for patients with symptoms of acute respiratory infection, droplet precautions should be added to the standard precautions. Airborne precautions must be employed during any aerosol-generating procedures. Healthcare facilities managing patients suspected or confirmed to have MERS-CoV should adopt appropriate measures to minimize the risk of virus transmission to other patients, healthcare workers (both medical and service personnel), and visitors. These measures include interventions at the patient-care interface and general practices such as proper linen management, thorough cleaning and disinfection, and effective waste management. When caring for probable or confirmed MERS-CoV cases, contact precautions and eye protection should be added to the standard precautions. Airborne precautions should also be applied during aerosol-generating procedures. Hospital cleaning staff must be informed and trained to take appropriate precautions when cleaning the rooms of MERS-CoV patients. Individuals at high risk of developing severe disease (e.g., those over 60 years of age, or with diabetes, renal failure, chronic lung disease, or immunocompromised conditions) should take precautions when visiting farms or markets where dromedary camels are present or engaging in activities involving close contact with dromedary camels, particularly in the Middle East and Africa. These precautions include avoiding contact with camels, refraining from consuming raw camel milk or urine, and ensuring camel meat is thoroughly cooked before consumption. Studies conducted in the Arabian Peninsula, West and North Africa, and the Horn of Africa indicate that individuals handling or working with dromedary camels are at an increased risk of MERS-CoV infection compared to those without camel contact. Until more evidence is available, camel farm workers, slaughterhouse workers, market workers, veterinarians, and others handling dromedary camels should practice good personal hygiene, including frequent handwashing with soap and water or alcohol-based hand gel before and after animal contact. Workers should wear facial protection when feasible, as well as protective clothing and boots, which should be removed after work (followed by hand hygiene) and washed daily. Workers should avoid exposing family members to soiled work clothing, shoes, or other items that may have come into contact with camel secretions or excretions. Such items should remain at the workplace for daily washing, and workers should have access to and use shower facilities at their workplaces before leaving the premises. Dromedary camels infected with MERS-CoV may not exhibit any signs of infection, making it impossible to determine whether an animal at a farm, market, racetrack, or slaughterhouse is shedding the virus capable of infecting humans. However, infected animals may excrete MERS-CoV through nasal and eye discharge, feces, and potentially in their milk and urine. The virus may also be present in the raw organs and meat of infected animals. Therefore, until more is known about animal infections, the best protection is to practice good hygiene and avoid direct contact with these sources. Sick dromedary camels should never be slaughtered for consumption, and dead camels should be safely buried or destroyed. Without adequate personal protective equipment, individuals should avoid contact with any dromedary camel that has recently tested positive for MERS-CoV until subsequent tests confirm the animal is free of infection. Health officials in countries outside the affected regions should maintain a high level of vigilance, particularly in nations with significant numbers of travelers or migrant workers returning from the Middle East. Surveillance should be enhanced in these countries in accordance with WHO guidelines, alongside the implementation of infection prevention and control procedures in healthcare facilities. WHO continues to request that Member States report all confirmed and probable cases, along with information about their exposures, testing, and clinical course, to inform the most effective international preparedness and response strategies. WHO does not currently recommend special screening at points of entry for MERS-CoV nor the application of any travel or trade restrictions. WHO guidelines and tools for epidemiologic investigations are available on the WHO MERS-CoV website.
